summary: Liam Hampton addresses the proliferation of AI agents across tools and the misconception that one-shot prompts solve all problems. He presents a framework of three agent types accessible from VS Code as a single control plane. Local agents run on the developer's machine with remote models, offering hands-on, human-in-the-loop iteration—ideal for writing tests. Background agents use Git worktrees, branches mapped to isolated subdirectories, enabling 50/50 involvement for larger tasks like building a front end. Cloud agents run in GitHub Actions within isolated environments, with built-in safeguards including network firewalls and no direct push access to the main branch. They have extended context through MCP servers, including the GitHub MCP server and Playwright MCP server for automated front-end testing with screenshots. Cloud agents are suited for fully hands-off tasks like documentation or making a repo open source friendly. Hampton demonstrates all three on a Python CRUD product store, running them concurrently. He initiates a background agent via Copilot CLI with Autopilot (in preview) to create a front end UI from GitHub issue 25. Simultaneously, he launches a cloud agent to add README and contribution guidelines, and uses a local agent with Claude Opus 4.6 to write unit tests, discovering error-handling issues and iterating hands-on. He then shows VS Code's customization modal, exposing agents (custom and built-in like ask, explore, plan), skills (extensions, address PR comments, create pull request), instructions, prompts, hooks, and MCP servers in one place. These concepts—custom instructions, custom agents, prompt files, and agent skills—apply across GitHub Copilot and other AI services. Third-party support includes Claude. Hampton highlights the Awesome Copilot open-source project (aka.ms/awesomecopilot) and explains MCP (Model Context Protocol) as a way to extend LLMs with access to cloud resources, testing tools, and documentation. He closes by reiterating VS Code as a single entry point for AI agents with first-party, third-party, and MCP support.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Hampton opens by polling the audience on Copilot and VS Code usage, then frames the problem: agents are everywhere, one-shot prompts don't work, ROI on AI spending remains unrealized, and token spend is a real concern driving creative workarounds.

sections.title: Three Agent Types and When to Use Each
sections.summary: Introduces local agents (hands-on, human in the loop, for tests), background agents (using Git worktrees, 50/50 involvement, for UI tasks), and cloud agents (scaling outside the org, fully hands-off, for documentation and open source friendliness). Explains Git worktrees as branches mapped to isolated subdirectories.

sections.title: VS Code as Single Entry Point
sections.summary: Positions VS Code as a unified control plane supporting local, background, cloud, and third-party agents, with the goal of reducing developer cognitive load by meeting developers where they already work.

sections.title: Demo: One Codebase, Three Problems, Three Agents
sections.summary: Walks through a video demo on a Python CRUD app. Starts a background agent with Autopilot to build a front end from GitHub issue 25, pausing before PR. Simultaneously launches a cloud agent to make the repo open source friendly. Then uses a local agent with Claude Opus 4.6 to write unit tests and fix error handling, iterating hands-on. All three agents run concurrently within VS Code.

sections.title: How Cloud Agents Work
sections.summary: Explains that cloud agents run in GitHub Actions within isolated, secure environments. They have extended context through MCP servers including GitHub MCP server and Playwright MCP server for front-end testing with screenshots. Built-in safeguards include network firewalls with whitelisted endpoints and no direct push access to the main branch.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Agent Concepts
sections.summary: Clarifies that while the demo uses GitHub Copilot, the same concepts apply across all AI agents: custom instructions defining agent behavior, custom agents for specific tasks, prompt files for prompting assistance, and agent skills as the newer version of agents.md.

sections.title: VS Code Customization Modal
sections.summary: Demonstrates VS Code's customization modal accessible via the Copilot chat pane cog icon, showing agents (custom test agent, built-in ask/explore/plan), skills (extensions, address PR comments, create pull request), instructions, prompts, hooks, and MCP servers all configurable from one place.

sections.title: Third-Party Support, Awesome Copilot, and MCP
sections.summary: Highlights third-party support including Claude within VS Code. Introduces the Awesome Copilot open-source project (aka.ms/awesomecopilot) for hands-on customization examples usable across AI tooling. Explains MCP (Model Context Protocol) as a way to extend LLMs with access to Azure, GCP, AWS resources and free services like Playwright and Microsoft Learn. Wraps up by reiterating VS Code as a single entry point for AI agents with first-party, third-party, and MCP support.
